analysis.one_liner: Bans selling goods and services at grossly excessive prices, with fines up to 5% of a big company's revenue.
analysis.headline: Introduced in February 2024 with 9 Senate cosponsors, the bill never received a committee vote and died when that Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it unlawful for any company in the supply chain to sell a good or service at a "grossly excessive price." During declared emergencies or other major market shocks, big companies would face a presumption of violation if they raised prices well above their own prior levels or competitors' prices, and they could only escape by proving with strong evidence that the increase came from costs beyond their control. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could sue violators, with civil penalties up to 5% of a parent company's annual revenue, and publicly traded companies would have to disclose their pricing strategies and margins to the SEC during market shocks.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, who would gain a federal backstop against price spikes during emergencies and other shocks, enforced by the FTC and state attorneys general and backed by penalties large enough to matter to big corporations.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes selling at a "grossly excessive price" unlawful for any seller, no matter where it sits in the supply chain, and during exceptional market shocks creates a presumption of violation for sellers charging more than their own prior 120-day average or more than competitors in the market.

The FTC could sue violators directly in federal court for injunctions, restitution for consumers, and civil penalties of up to 5% of a parent company's annual revenue; state attorneys general could bring the same suits on behalf of their residents.

Publicly traded companies would have to disclose in SEC filings, during quarters with market shocks, how much of their revenue increase came from price versus volume, their gross margins, and a detailed explanation of their pricing strategy when prices rose faster than costs.
Companies whose ultimate parent earns under $100 million a year in U.S. revenue are exempt unless they raise prices for reasons beyond their control, shielding small businesses.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations — major retailers, grocers, energy suppliers, and other big sellers — would bear civil penalties up to 5% of parent-company revenue, the burden of proving price increases came from uncontrollable costs, and new SEC disclosure work during market shocks. The bill also appropriates $1 billion to the FTC to enforce it, from the Treasury.

drawbacks.text: The central standard — a "grossly excessive price" — is left for the FTC to define after enactment (the bill suggests it might start at 120% of the prior six-month market average), so legitimate price increases could face enforcement even with a defense that requires proving costs were beyond the seller's control.

During a market shock, a company is presumed in violation if it charged more than its own prior 120-day average, and can only rebut that presumption with clear and convincing evidence — a high bar — that the increase was directly attributable to costs outside its control, which could penalize sellers whose costs genuinely rose but who cannot document it to that standard.

The bill appropriates $1 billion of new federal money to the FTC and creates new SEC reporting requirements for any public company that prices through a market shock, a real compliance cost that would ultimately run through prices and investor returns.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the benefit is a federal backstop against emergency-driven price spikes, with the enforcement teeth (penalties up to 5% of parent revenue and state AG lawsuits) needed to make it real. The costs are real but design trade-offs rather than fatal flaws: the definition of an excessive price is deferred to FTC rulemaking, the rebuttal standard during shocks is strict, and the bill adds heavy disclosure and penalty exposure for large firms. An honest supporter would acknowledge that the breadth of the standard could chill some lawful pricing and that the economics of supply shocks are hard to adjudicate in real time.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, which never took it up; it got related hearings in the Banking Committee but no markup, no vote, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on February 26, 2024, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
Nine senators cosponsored — 8 Democrats and 1 independent; no Republican signed on.

In May 2024 the Senate Banking Committee and its Economic Policy Subcommittee held hearings printed as S.Hrg. 118-646 and S.Hrg. 118-556 that appear in the bill's action history, but the Commerce Committee, which held the referral, never acted.
No further action was taken before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations and major retailers — no federal price-gouging ban, FTC or state AG enforcement, or new SEC pricing disclosures took effect, so their pricing during emergencies and inflationary periods remains governed only by scattered state laws.

for.name: Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its push, with the FTC price-gouging ban, state AG enforcement, and SEC pricing disclosures as its core provisions.

for.name: 8 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a small all-Democratic bloc of support.

for.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
for.role: Senate committee that held related hearings
for.what_they_did: Held hearings printed as S.Hrg. 118-646 in May 2024, and its Economic Policy Subcommittee held hearings printed as S.Hrg. 118-556, actions recorded in the bill's history.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the referred bill
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral on the day it was introduced — no markup, no committee vote — and it died with the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All nine cosponsors were Senate Democrats or independents; no Republican sponsored or supported the bill, and it never reached a vote where a party split could be recorded.

industries.note: Sellers with more than $100 million in parent revenue would face a presumption of price gouging during market shocks if they charged above their prior 120-day average, with civil penalties up to 5% of parent-company revenue. Their interest in keeping prices above pre-shock levels runs directly against consumers paying those prices.

industries.industry: Large consumer goods and energy suppliers
industries.note: The ban applies at every point in the supply chain, so wholesalers and suppliers raising prices during shortages or emergencies would face FTC and state AG suits and restitution orders. Consumers pay the prices the bill targets.

Covered issuers would have to report in SEC filings how much of revenue growth came from price versus volume, their gross margins, and the rationale for raising prices faster than costs. That is a real compliance burden, but the disclosures mainly serve investors and the public's ability to see whether margins — not costs — drove price increases.

Companies whose ultimate parent earns under $100 million a year are exempt from the ban unless they raise prices for reasons beyond their control, giving them relative protection while large competitors face penalties.
The bill gives state AGs a new federal cause of action to sue for penalties and restitution on behalf of their residents, parallel to the FTC's enforcement.
